title: AI Changes the Data Interface, Not the Query Engine
gist: Peihao Yuan argues AI agents change the data interface, not the query engine: in a disaster-recovery analysis of 1,523 services (1.13M rows, 3.8 MB of Parquet), DuckDB computed deterministic fact packets and the agent only interpreted them. He proposes a determinism split, a replay bundle for reproducibility, and four signals for when an embedded engine must give way to a managed lakehouse.

insights.claim: An AI agent that reads Parquet still depends on an execution engine: AI changes the analytical interface and interpretation layer, not the need for precise computation.
insights.speaker: Peihao Yuan
insights.so_what: Do not assume agents make query engines or lakehouses obsolete; the engine becomes an embedded component.
insights.quote: The engine remains; the interface changes.
insights.locator: An AI agent that reads Parquet still depends on an execution engine

insights.claim: In the disaster-recovery exercise prototype, thirty-second service metrics were stored as Parquet in S3-compatible storage, DuckDB did deterministic aggregation and an AI agent classified failover outcomes, working without a shared lakehouse.
insights.speaker: Peihao Yuan
insights.so_what: Shows a lightweight stack sufficient for focused agent analytics.
insights.locator: We encountered this question while automating the analysis of a large disaster-recovery exercise.

insights.claim: The agent generates only the analytical query; an allowlist validator rejects non-allowlisted tables or non-read-only operations, the query runs in a sandbox, and application code normalizes rows into a fact packet the model receives instead of inventing values.
insights.speaker: Peihao Yuan
insights.so_what: Guardrails around generated SQL are the control layer for agent analytics in production.
insights.locator: In this simplified example, the agent generates only the analytical query.

insights.claim: The determinism split assigns filtering, aggregation, joins, sorting, window calculations and data quality checks to the engine, and evidence selection, classification, investigation suggestions and abstaining when evidence is insufficient to the agent.
insights.speaker: Peihao Yuan
insights.so_what: A reusable rule for dividing work between engines and models.
insights.quote: separate exact computation from contextual reasoning
insights.locator: The most reusable lesson from the project

insights.claim: Using an LLM as a query engine to read hundreds of thousands of rows and compute counts, percentiles or averages is an anti-pattern: it is slow, token-expensive, hard to reproduce and assigns deterministic work to a probabilistic system.
insights.speaker: Peihao Yuan
insights.so_what: Avoid pushing raw rows into model context; supply computed facts.
insights.locator: This division avoids a common anti-pattern, using an LLM as a query engine.

insights.claim: The agent adds value by resolving context-dependent, conflicting evidence, such as a service that absorbs traffic but depends on a near-saturated downstream, or a Tier-2 async backlog that would warrant escalation in a Tier-0 synchronous service, that would otherwise need an ever-growing set of service-specific rules.
insights.speaker: Peihao Yuan
insights.so_what: LLM judgement can replace brittle rule sets when deterministic facts underpin it.
insights.locator: More importantly, some cases contained conflicting evidence

insights.claim: Judging a failover requires context: a QPS rise may be too small to absorb lost traffic, a lower success rate may reflect expected business rejections, and a latency spike at cutover may be harmless, so the team used a previous-day baseline, an hour-before baseline and a post-cutover steady-state window.
insights.speaker: Peihao Yuan
insights.so_what: Baselines and steady-state windows reduce false failures in resilience testing.

insights.claim: In the example, the surviving region absorbed about 76% of expected failover traffic (910 of 1,200 QPS), success rate was 99.41% against a 99.90% SLO and p99 latency stayed elevated for 18 minutes, so the agent classified a partial failover and recommended reviewing routing capacity and downstream limits.
insights.speaker: Peihao Yuan
insights.so_what: Partial failover is a more actionable class than binary pass/fail.
insights.locator: For one service, the deterministic execution layer produced a fact packet

insights.claim: The exercise dataset had 1,127,748 fact rows across 1,523 services at about 3.8 MB of compressed Parquet, small enough for an embedded engine, and row count alone is not a reason to deploy a distributed lakehouse.
insights.speaker: Peihao Yuan
insights.so_what: Architecture should follow measured workload rather than the 'big data' label.
insights.quote: architecture decisions should follow the actual workload rather than the label big data

insights.claim: Each exercise had a self-describing S3 directory with index.json, manifest.json (schema, row counts, sizes, checksums), exercise_config.json, metrics Parquet files and a service dimension file, because a folder of files is not yet a trustworthy data asset.
insights.speaker: Peihao Yuan
insights.so_what: Manifests and checksums make file-based data assets verifiable.
insights.locator: The manifest was important because a folder of files is not yet a trustworthy data asset.

insights.claim: DuckDB suited the job because it runs in-process alongside the agent, reads Parquet directly with filter and column pushdown, provides SQL semantics and can spill to local storage, though it is not claimed to beat Spark, Trino or a managed lakehouse universally.
insights.speaker: Peihao Yuan
insights.so_what: Embedded engines lower the infrastructure cost of agent-driven analytics.
insights.locator: The point was not that DuckDB is universally better than Spark, Trino

insights.claim: A per-exercise replay bundle retained Parquet inputs, manifest, configuration, generated SQL or Python, execution metadata, derived facts, model output, agent version and prompt, and model identifier, enabling offline reruns, disputed-conclusion review and agent-version comparison.
insights.speaker: Peihao Yuan
insights.so_what: Auditability and replay make agent analytics defensible in production.
insights.locator: For every exercise, we retained a replay bundle containing:

insights.claim: Missing values need explicit semantics: missing QPS or error counts may mean zero activity, but missing success-rate or latency usually means no traffic to measure, and filling zeros would create false failures and false recoveries.
insights.speaker: Peihao Yuan
insights.so_what: Data-quality flags in the schema prevent silent misinterpretation by engine and agent.
insights.locator: We also encoded data semantics explicitly.

themes.theme: When to move to a lakehouse

insights.claim: Four signals mark the end of the lightweight architecture: independent consumers needing a stable catalog contract, data too large to move (terabyte scale), joins with large shared authoritative datasets, and concurrent writes or table-level evolution.
insights.speaker: Peihao Yuan
insights.so_what: A concrete checklist for deciding when to add shared data infrastructure.
insights.locator: Four signals indicate where the lightweight architecture begins to encounter pressure.

insights.claim: A managed lakehouse combines a catalog (discovery, ownership, permissions), an open table format such as Apache Iceberg (snapshots, schema evolution, safe writes) and a shared query engine, but adds integration, governance, compute and operational cost, so adopt it for real sharing, scale and transaction needs, not on day one.
insights.speaker: Peihao Yuan
insights.so_what: Avoid over-engineering AI projects with platform costs before sharing or scale require them.
